tweets.text: Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin . I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic. That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it. I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits: 1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed. 2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it. 3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do. 4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this. 5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future. 6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent. 7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it. 8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company. 9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund. All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking. For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option. I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent. But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years. I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better. Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so. Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way. Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change. Nathan Calvin (@_NathanCalvin) Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate. However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic. (Fair warning: this response is a bit long) To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world? One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion. Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in): “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.” There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet… incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…” A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same. Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside. When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at. 2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development. 3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?) 4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public. 5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance. 6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments. 7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.” 8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords. 9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems. Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization). But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization). When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong? A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount. I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release: “Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives. That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.” I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons). — https://nitter.kareem.one/_NathanCalvin/status/2112295219765137570#m

Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. we've found and have been working on disclosure for a remote code execution in a widely-deployed compression library. it's both an impactful issue and an example that shows how complicated it can be to coordinate patching, since it's integrated into a lot of downstream software: OpenAI (@OpenAI) During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy. The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server. This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE. We've been building tools around our frontier cyber models, which have secured us far beyond what we could have unassisted and should generalize as key to how defenders secure themselves going forward. OpenAI (@OpenAI) Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications. On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments. While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software. After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. actu.text_fr: 1/2 Merci Gavin pour un échange particulièrement réfléchi. Je ne passe généralement pas beaucoup de temps sur les réseaux sociaux, mais je voulais m'engager ici car cela met vraiment en évidence le cœur d'une conversation importante. Premièrement, concernant la réglementation, je pense que « la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la réglementation ou la distribuer largement » est un faux dilemme. Je sais qu'il existe une sorte de langage codé de la Silicon Valley où réglementation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir, mais j'ai toujours trouvé cela une image trop simplifiée du monde. Beaucoup de gens en dehors de cette bulle considèrent la réglementation comme quelque chose qui contraint le pouvoir des entreprises et profite aux gens ordinaires. Je ne suis pas nécessairement d'accord avec cette perspective non plus, plutôt je pense que c'est compliqué et dépend vraiment de ce qu'est la "réglementation". Mais en particulier, je pense que ceux qui adhèrent au cadre "réglementation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir" sous-estiment souvent le pouvoir décentralisateur des processus institutionnels objectifs et équitables. Une analogie grossière est que le système judiciaire formel peut parfois sembler guindé et élitiste, mais il fait un bien meilleur travail pour défendre les droits des individus vulnérables que l'alternative, la justice populaire. À leur meilleur, les institutions peuvent investir le pouvoir dans les idées plutôt que dans les personnes, et ainsi décentraliser ce pouvoir. C'est pourquoi Anthropic a toujours élaboré ses propositions de politique très soigneusement. Nous nous efforçons de faire des propositions qui désavantagent (ralentissent) les entreprises d'IA de pointe tout en *avantageant* les concurrents plus petits. Le SB53 de Californie (que nous avons soutenu), et même le SB 1047, largement décrié (sur lequel nous étions ambivalents), exemptent complètement toute entreprise en dessous d'un certain montant de revenus ou de coûts d'entraînement de modèles d'être couverte du tout (c'était 500 millions de dollars pour le SB 53, moins pour le SB 1047 mais nous nous y sommes opposés). Plus récemment, le processus de test que nous avons préconisé à CAISI et à la Maison Blanche implique des tests plus rigoureux pour les modèles de pointe que pour les modèles hors frontière – quelque chose qui avantage différentiellement les challengers. De même, la lettre « Pacing the Frontier » envisage (ou du moins, l'implémentation préférée d'Anthropic l'envisage) de moduler le rythme des meilleurs modèles tout en ne contraignant pas ceux qui rattrapent. Cela nuit aux intérêts commerciaux des laboratoires de pointe et aide les challengers, y compris les modèles open-weights ! Dans l'ensemble, mon point de vue est que l'IA est *structurellement* une technologie qui tend à concentrer le pouvoir, pour des raisons qui n'ont rien à voir avec la réglementation (plus à voir avec les implications extrêmes des lois d'échelle). Les modèles open-weights aident à cela, mais ne sont en aucun cas une solution suffisante car ils déplacent simplement la concentration vers ceux qui ont le plus de puissance de calcul et de puces (qui sont à peu près les laboratoires de pointe, plus peut-être les fournisseurs de matériel). Par contraste, je pense que les bonnes « règles de la route » peuvent simultanément (a) aborder les risques de cyber/bio/alignement de l'IA, (b) contraindre institutionnellement le pouvoir des entreprises d'IA de pointe, et (c) laisser de la place aux modèles open-weights tout en abordant les risques spécifiques qu'ils apportent. PS : Je ne pense pas que les événements des derniers mois aient « échoué à aboutir à [mon] chemin réglementaire préféré ». L'approche que l'administration Trump semble adopter – tests avant déploiement pour les modèles de pointe, et aussi tests des modèles open-weights lorsqu'ils se rapprochent de la frontière – est une approche que je soutiens très fortement, bien que bien sûr je doive voir les détails pour être sûr. Je soutiens également les idées de Demis Hassabis concernant une entité de type FINRA. Cela contraste avec il y a six mois, lorsque la plupart de l'industrie prônait encore la préemption de toute réglementation étatique et aucune approche fédérale apparente.
actu.text_original: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.
actu.decryptage: Dario Amodei explique que la réglementation de l'IA ne doit pas nécessairement concentrer le pouvoir mais peut au contraire le décentraliser si elle est bien conçue. Il soutient une approche qui favorise les petites entreprises et les modèles open-source tout en gérant les risques.

actu.text_fr: 2/2 Deuxièmement, sur la communication autour de l'IA. Je ne suis pas d'accord pour dire que ma communication a été disproportionnellement négative. En fait, elle a été à peu près équilibrée entre les risques et les avantages : j'ai écrit un essai majeur sur chacun, et même dans les interviews où je discute des risques, je veille à mentionner fréquemment les avantages incroyables ainsi qu'à proposer des solutions possibles aux risques (les courts clips d'interviews qui finissent sur les réseaux sociaux ont tendance à être disproportionnellement négatifs, car cela génère des clics). En fait, j'ai écrit 'Machines of Loving Grace' parce que je ne pensais pas que l'industrie de l'IA présentait une image suffisamment inspirante de la manière dont la technologie pourrait radicalement transformer le monde pour le mieux. La majeure partie de l'essai est consacrée à réfuter le scepticisme quant au potentiel de l'IA dans la santé et la biologie, et à montrer pourquoi je pense qu'il sera en fait possible de guérir la plupart des maladies humaines en environ 5 à 10 ans, aussi fou que cela puisse paraître aux gens ordinaires et franchement aux biologistes aussi (j'en étais un !). Et, si vous lisez mon essai le plus récent (Policy on the AI Exponential), je discute de propositions concrètes sur la manière de rationaliser le processus de la FDA pour garantir que le déluge de médicaments accélérés par l'IA ne soit pas ralenti par le processus réglementaire. Je ressens l'urgence ici : j'ai perdu mon père d'une hépatite C quelques années seulement avant le développement des antiviraux à action directe (sofosbuvir), qui guérissent 95% des patients et l'auraient probablement guéri. Je suis d'accord pour dire que le public a une vision négative de l'IA (et que c'est un gros problème), mais je ne pense pas que cela soit principalement causé par moi ou par tout autre dirigeant de l'IA qui met en garde contre les risques de l'IA. Je pense que c'est fondamentalement une crise de confiance. Je pense que les gens ordinaires ne font pas confiance aux entreprises, aux gouvernements ou à l'industrie technologique et soupçonnent toujours que nous préparons une nouvelle façon de les arnaquer. Les causes de cela remontent à des décennies et l'IA n'en est que la dernière itération. Je ne pense pas qu'une campagne marketing clinquante avec une image positive (ce que certains ont préconisé qu'Anthropic fasse) soit le moyen de regagner cette confiance - à ce stade, dire que l'IA va guérir le cancer est plus un cliché qu'inspirant, et la plupart des gens pensent que c'est trompeur. Ce qui fonctionnera, c'est de *guérir réellement le cancer*. Je pense que la critique la plus juste des entreprises d'IA, y compris Anthropic, est que nous n'avons pas encore tenu nos grandes promesses de bénéficier au monde. C'est entièrement de notre faute, et je pense que c'est la critique que vous devriez faire, au lieu de tout ce qui concerne la communication et le marketing. Nous faisons cependant de notre mieux pour y remédier : Anthropic intensifie rapidement ses efforts en biologie et en médecine, et nous espérons avoir des résultats incroyables dans les années à venir et quelques lueurs précoces dans les mois à venir. Lorsque nous aurons réellement accompli quelque chose, le monde entier l'apprendra, aussi fort que possible, je vous le promets. Mais d'ici là, je ne veux pas faire de promesses en l'air, et en attendant, je me sens obligé de parler honnêtement des risques très réels de l'IA et de la manière d'y remédier. L'honnêteté est la bonne voie sur le fond, et en termes de crédibilité et de confiance du public, elle n'est pas pire, et peut même être meilleure, qu'une approche qui ignore ou détourne l'attention des risques que les gens comprennent instinctivement comme étant réels.
actu.text_original: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.
actu.decryptage: Dario Amodei défend sa communication sur les risques de l'IA, la jugeant nécessaire et honnête. Il insiste sur le fait que le vrai progrès viendra des réalisations concrètes, comme la guérison de maladies, plutôt que du marketing, et qu'Anthropic travaille activement dans ce sens.

actu.text_fr: Mistral a sorti de nouveaux modèles de parole ! Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 prend la 3ème place du classement Speech to Text d'Artificial Analysis, et Voxtral 3 TTS entre dans le top 12 dans les deux arènes Text to Speech @MistralAI a publié Voxtral 3 : un nouveau modèle Text to Speech et trois modèles Speech to Text (Small Transcribe 3, Mini Transcribe 3 et Mini Transcribe Realtime 3). Nous les avons tous évalués. Points clés : ➤ Speech to Text : Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 prend la 3ème place du classement Artificial Analysis Speech to Text avec un indice AA-WER de 2,1 %, devant ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (2,2 %) et Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 (2,3 %). Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 se classe 5ème avec 2,2 %. ➤ Streaming Speech to Text : Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 obtient un AA-WER de transcript final de 3,3 % au réglage de 960 ms (6ème sur 46) et 3,6 % à 480 ms, contre 5,2 % pour le précédent Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime. ➤ Text to Speech, Voix Fournisseur : Voxtral 3 TTS obtient un Elo de 1 218 sur 1 599 apparitions dans l'arène, se classant 12ème sur 98, juste derrière Breeze TTS 2 à 1 221 et devant Inworld Realtime TTS-2 Flash et StepAudio 2.5 TTS à 1 216. Il se classe 13ème en Anglais (US) et 12ème en Anglais (UK). ➤ Text to Speech, Voix Contrôlée : Voxtral 3 TTS obtient 1 068 sur 1 614 apparitions, se classant 12ème sur 43 avec les mêmes 8 voix clonées, derrière Eleven v3 à 1 072 et à égalité avec Ming-3.0-tts d'Ant Group à 1 068. Il se classe 10ème en Assistants et 10ème en Anglais (UK). ➤ Robustesse de la Prononciation : Voxtral 3 TTS obtient 84,4 %, se classant 13ème sur 32 modèles, derrière Qwen-Audio-3.1-TTS-Plus à 84,6 % et devant HeyGen Voice à 83,2 %. Il se classe 3ème en Termes Autonomes à 93,9 %. ➤ Prix : Voxtral 3 TTS est proposé à 13 $/1M de caractères, contre Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS à 16,5 $/1M de caractères, Eleven v4 Turbo à 40 $/1M de caractères et Simba 3.2 à 6,6 $/1M de caractères. Voir plus de détails et écouter des exemples ci-dessous ⬇️

tips.text_fr: nous avons trouvé et travaillons sur la divulgation d'une exécution de code à distance dans une bibliothèque de compression largement déployée. c'est à la fois un problème impactant et un exemple qui montre à quel point il peut être compliqué de coordonner la correction, car elle est intégrée dans de nombreux logiciels en aval : OpenAI (@OpenAI) Lors de cet exercice de 'red-teaming', nous avons également trouvé une vulnérabilité qui permet une exécution de code à distance sans authentification dans Brotli, une bibliothèque de compression largement déployée incluse dans de nombreux logiciels tels que Node.js, Bun et Envoy. La faille pourrait permettre à un attaquant d'exécuter son propre code sur les systèmes affectés en envoyant ou en répondant avec des données compressées malveillantes, sans avoir besoin de créer un compte utilisateur. Autrement dit, un serveur non corrigé qui accepte une entrée compressée pourrait être détourné par un client malveillant, et un client non corrigé qui accepte une entrée compressée (comme "curl --compressed") pourrait être détourné par un serveur malveillant. Ce problème de cause profonde a été corrigé dans le code source de Brotli en février, mais il n'était pas connu à l'époque qu'il donnait lieu à une vulnérabilité de sécurité et il n'y a pas eu de version plus récente de Brotli. Comme Brotli est intégré dans d'autres logiciels, tout logiciel qui inclut cette bibliothèque doit également prendre la mise à jour, suivie par les utilisateurs de ce logiciel. Nous avons divulgué la vulnérabilité à Brotli et à d'autres projets en aval tels que Node.js, qui ont publié ou publient actuellement des mises à jour de sécurité, et Brotli a publié de nouvelles versions et un CVE. Plus de détails sur le correctif et les solutions de contournement ci-dessous : patchtheplanet.org/brotli Lien Vulnérabilité Brotli (CVE-2026-111497) — Patch the Planet Brotli decoder vulnerability: affected software, fixed releases, and how to disable Brotli decoding while you patch. patchtheplanet.org — http://nitter.meowing.monster/OpenAI/status/2113766354386084338#m
tips.text_original: we've found and have been working on disclosure for a remote code execution in a widely-deployed compression library. it's both an impactful issue and an example that shows how complicated it can be to coordinate patching, since it's integrated into a lot of downstream software: OpenAI (@OpenAI) During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy. The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server. This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE. More details on the patch and mitigations below: patchtheplanet.org/brotli Link Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) — Patch the Planet Brotli decoder vulnerability: affected software, fixed releases, and how to disable Brotli decoding while you patch. patchtheplanet.org — http://nitter.meowing.monster/OpenAI/status/2113766354386084338#m

tips.text_fr: Une publication sur la manière dont nous avons sécurisé notre environnement d'entraînement de modèles de pointe. Nous avons développé des outils autour de nos modèles cyber de pointe, qui nous ont permis d'assurer une sécurité bien au-delà de ce que nous aurions pu faire sans aide et qui devraient se généraliser comme clé pour la manière dont les défenseurs s'assurent eux-mêmes à l'avenir. OpenAI (@OpenAI) Au cours des derniers mois, nous avons considérablement renforcé la sécurité de notre environnement d'entraînement de recherche. Nous avons supprimé l'accès à Internet en direct pour tous les modèles de pointe pendant l'entraînement et avons construit un monde hors ligne pour qu'ils l'utilisent à la place – une version mise en cache du web où ils peuvent toujours apprendre à naviguer, rechercher et utiliser des applications. Le 20 septembre, après qu'un modèle a exploité une mauvaise configuration DNS pour trouver un moyen de sortir de ce monde hors ligne, nous avons interrompu l'entraînement de pointe pour renforcer davantage le confinement. Nous avons assemblé des équipes d'agents, alimentées par nos modèles les plus capables en cyber, et leur avons confié la tâche de trouver des faiblesses dans nos environnements de recherche. Bien qu'ils n'aient trouvé aucune voie vers Internet qu'ils pourraient facilement exploiter tout en dissimulant leurs activités à nos moniteurs, ils ont trouvé des vulnérabilités zero-day, des évasions de machines virtuelles et des canaux latéraux matériels pour la communication entre agents. Nous avons utilisé leurs découvertes pour renforcer davantage nos défenses et contribuer à des correctifs pour les logiciels open source. Après avoir renforcé notre architecture de confinement, nous avons repris notre entraînement et notre inférence RL de pointe le 1er octobre. Nous avons réservé une puissance de calcul substantielle pour le 'red-teaming' continu, et avons fait du 'red-teaming' à haute puissance de calcul une partie des cas de sécurité que nous utilisons pour décider si l'entraînement et l'évaluation de pointe peuvent procéder en toute sécurité. openai.com/index/securing-ou… Lien Sécurisation de notre environnement d'entraînement de modèles de pointe OpenAI explique comment nous avons renforcé le confinement pour l'entraînement et l'évaluation de modèles de pointe, y compris les environnements hors ligne et le red-teaming à haute puissance de calcul. openai.com — http://nitter.meowing.monster/OpenAI/status/2113718797505036665#m
tips.text_original: A post on how we've been securing our frontier model training environment. We've been building tools around our frontier cyber models, which have secured us far beyond what we could have unassisted and should generalize as key to how defenders secure themselves going forward. OpenAI (@OpenAI) Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications. On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments. While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software. After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely. openai.com/index/securing-ou… Link Securing our frontier model training environment OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming. openai.com — http://nitter.meowing.monster/OpenAI/status/2113718797505036665#m

idees.text_fr: Je ne veux pas rallumer le conflit, mais les événements de février 2026 sont un exemple frappant. Il est clair que notre position publique aurait pu gravement nuire à l'avenir de l'entreprise. Nous avons continué à plaider fermement en faveur des contrôles à l'exportation sur les puces et les équipements de fabrication de puces vers la Chine, car nous pensons que cela permet aux démocraties de négocier à partir d'une position de force sur les accords de sécurité de l'IA. Nous l'avons fait malgré les problèmes qu'elle nous a créés avec des partenaires industriels qui ont des points de vue très différents et dont nous dépendons fortement. Pour autant que je sache, nous avons été la première, et toujours la seule, entreprise de pointe à restreindre la vente de services d'IA aux entreprises contrôlées par la RPC, y compris celles qui opèrent par l'intermédiaire de pays tiers (sinon une échappatoire majeure). Nous avons donc renoncé à des affaires importantes à court terme pour éviter d'alimenter des plateformes et des applications d'IA qui aideraient les services militaires et de renseignement du PCC. Nous nous attaquons également à la distillation ; en général, la distillation ne représente pas une menace majeure pour nous sur le plan commercial, mais comme les exportations de puces, elle a des implications préoccupantes pour la sécurité nationale et la sûreté, nous déployons donc beaucoup d'énergie et de ressources de l'entreprise pour y remédier.
